Acceptance summary:

This manuscript uses an animal model, the zebrafish, to identify mutations that increase nicotine preference. The authors then proceed to identify variants of the same gene in humans and report correlations with smoking. The combined observations in two so distantly related species adds strength to the findings.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Identification of Slit3 as a locus affecting nicotine preference in zebrafish and human smoking behaviour" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Lars Westberg (Reviewer #1); Karl Clark (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary

Genetic contributions to smoking behaviour were sought by screening mutagenized zebrafish for nicotine place preference. A SNP in the Slit3 gene was identified among 300 predicted loss of function mutants. Two human cohorts with SNP variants in the SLIT3 gene showed correlation with cigarette consumption and likelihood of cessation. Zebrafish larvae with Slit3 mutations displayed altered behavioural sensitivity to amisulpride, an antagonist at dopamine and serotonin receptors. Larvae had increased mRNA of receptor 5htr1aaNo effect on neuronal. These findings show a role for SLIT3 signalling in development of pathways involved in nicotine effects.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers and myself as reviewing editor find this to be an interesting study but we request more details to evaluate the robustness of the findings as detailed below. We also request more discussion of the suggested role of monoamines for slitr3 actions on nicotine preference and improved description of the human genetic study.

1) Please provide more quantitative parameters in the Abstract and also state clearly in what direction the nicotine preference was affected: Out of 25 identified inactivating mutations, one in the Slit3 gene segregated with increased nicotine preference in heterozygous individuals.

2) Explain in the Abstract why amisulpride was tested: "...dopaminergic and serotonergic antagonist known to affect startle reflex which is correlated with addiction..."

3) Say in what direction amisulpride affected the behavior.

4) Has amisulpride been demonstrated to have the same receptor preference and effect (antagonist) in zebrafish as in human? Amisulpride was not used in the zebrafish study in reference 46. Discussion paragraph five says that "acoustic startle is sensitive to modulation of dopaminergic and serotonergic signalling in all species studied", but as the three references provided concern only three species (human, mouse and zebrafish), it is better to say "in the three species studied".

5) The results from the mutant screen showing an association between slitr3 and nicotine preference in zebrafish seems convincing, although it is based on a moderate number of fish. Please consider presenting this result as a main finding in the Abstract and Discussion, rather than the tentative associations from the human genetic study.

6) The results from the pharmacological and qPCR experiments are interesting but deserves a more thorough discussion on how the findings using the D2 antagonist amisulpride, fits together with the difference in htr1aa expression and lack of difference in TH expression.

7) The benefits and the limitations of using zebrafish of various ages in the different experiments (behavioral, IHC, qPCR vs. pharmacology) should be more clearly addressed.

8) The method used for quantification of the immunostainings should be described. It is not possible to exclude group differences from the pictures in presented in Figure 5A-C.

9) Whole embryos were used for the qPCR study. This should be raised as a limitation, since many of the studied genes most likely are not brain-specific.

10) Motivate the chosen genes investigated with qPCR. For example, some of the crucial enzymes were not studied.

11) You may consider to compare serotonin neurons using the immunohistochemical approach they used for TH neurons in Figure 5.

12) Explain why different scales are used in Supplementary file 1–table 5A and B.

13) The description of the human genetic study needs to be improved. For example, the number of participants included from both of the genetic cohorts should be presented in Materials and methods (but also in Results, e.g. in Tables 1 and 2).

Furthermore, it is unclear if the Finish samples were genotyped by the authors or if data was received from somewhere. Also consider modifying the study design. It is not clear why the London sample was divided into heavy and light smokers. Already before splitting the sample the number of participants must be considered as low for a genetic study. With the current study design, very many tests were conducted, so the correction method for multiple testing correction must be presented (like Bonferroni for qPCR data). You may consider to use the London study as an exploratory cohort and the Finish study as a replication cohort. In the Finish cohort only SNPs significantly associated in the exploratory cohort would be investigated.

14) Explore to what extent SLIT3 gene variants have been associated with nicotine dependence and related phenotypes in previous GWA studies. One tool that may be helpful is the GWAS ATLAS (https://atlas.ctglab.nl).

15) It would be helpful if a picture was added for the gene with the SNP locations indicated, above the LD plot, in Figure 9.

16) Although Figure 5 is meant to show there are not gross abnormalities in axon pathfinding, I feel that there are observable differences between the WT and (Slit3+/- OR Slit3-/-) in acetylated tubulin staining. I am not sure if it is the particular panels chosen or a real but subtle difference. If there are similar individual differences between any 2 WT, it may be better to show 2 individuals for each genotype rather than the partial Z-stack that is in panel B. If it is a real, but subtle difference, it is better to discuss than try to pass off as the same.

17) The habituation data were found to be unconvincing. Most habituation in zebrafish larvae is a yes or no startle response and not based on distance travelled. However, these assays are typically earlier in development, so this may be a bit of an adaptation and could account for some of the differences. That being said, in Panel A the mean response based on your cutoff of 2.5 mm of movement does not reach habituation in your trial. This may lead to the less than spectacular differences in habituation rates. You probably want to be at a position where 80% of wild-type fish are showing habituation. This could be achieved by using more than 10 stimuli, decreasing the intensity of the stimuli, or changing the distance moved criteria. In other words, you may be too close to the arbitrary cutoff of 50% to be measuring real changes in habituation. So currently, the interpretation of these results may be a bit of a stretch. Even though statistical differences were measured, they may not be biologically relevant.

18) What were the overall results of this screen of 30 families? It is suggested that there were families with reduced nicotine CPP and increased nicotine CPP. Two mutations were described, but out of how many negative and positive effector families?

19) In Figure 3, the AJBQM2 line does not show significance in comparison to WT nor WT (nic) based on letter superscript (a), yet it is discussed as it does, including line "AJBQM2 differed from wildtype nicotine exposed fish but not wildtype saline controls." If it is not significantly different there are several places in the manuscript that are misleading.

claims.claim: Habituation to acoustic startle is known to involve catecholamine signalling.
claims.source: To further characterise the slit3 phenotype and explore potential functional differences in catecholamine circuitry, we examined the response and habituation to acoustic startle stimuli in wild type and mutant fish. results.result: The manuscript provides background on smoking genetics, noting that while smoking behavior has a strong genetic component, the field has been characterized by small effect sizes and lack of replication. The strongest evidence for causal effects is for functional variants in CHRNA5 and CYP2A6, while recent large studies have identified numerous new loci that remain to be biologically characterized.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by citations to established literature (WHO, 2017; Munafò et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Erzurumluoglu et al., 2019). These claims provide appropriate context for the study and accurately represent the current state of knowledge in smoking genetics research.

results.result: The manuscript describes limitations of QTL mapping approaches and introduces ENU mutagenesis as a method to overcome these limitations by generating stronger phenotypes than those occurring in natural populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 accurately describe established methodological approaches in genetic research. The limitations of QTL mapping and advantages of ENU mutagenesis are well-established in the field and appropriately cited (Crabbe, 2008).

results.result: The manuscript establishes that drug-induced reinforcement is conserved across species and that CPP is commonly used to measure drug reward. Previous ENU mutagenesis screens in zebrafish for cocaine/amphetamine-induced CPP have isolated lines with altered responses, but causal mutations have not been identified and predictive validity for human behavior has not been established.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 are well-supported by appropriate citations (Parker and Brennan, 2012; Tzschentke, 1998; Darland and Dowling, 2001; Ninkovic et al., 2006; Petzold et al., 2009). These claims accurately represent prior work and establish the gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

results.result: The manuscript establishes zebrafish as an appropriate model for nicotine research by documenting that zebrafish express homologues of all mammalian nicotinic acetylcholine receptors with similar binding characteristics, show robust CPP to nicotine, and develop dependence-related behaviors on prolonged exposure.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C26 are well-supported by multiple citations (Zirger et al., 2003; Ackerman et al., 2009; Pedersen et al., 2019; Papke et al., 2012; Ponzoni et al., 2014; Kily et al., 2008; Brock et al., 2017; Kedikian et al., 2013). These claims establish the translational relevance of the zebrafish model for studying nicotine responses.

results.result: Zebrafish showed robust CPP to nicotine (10 μM inducing 15-20% change in place preference), which was dose-dependently inhibited by varenicline and bupropion. Varenicline showed increasing inhibition at increasing concentrations, while bupropion inhibition was maximal at 1 μM and decreased at higher concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C29, C40-C42, C111-C113 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and consistent with previous findings (Ponzoni et al., 2014). The differential dose-response patterns for varenicline and bupropion are clearly demonstrated and appropriately interpreted as reflecting different modes of action. This validates the zebrafish CPP assay for nicotine research.

results.result: Nicotine-induced CPP was found to be heritable in zebrafish. Using 5 μM nicotine (predicted to induce minimal detectable CPP), the first generation showed normally distributed CPP change scores (mean 0.11, range -0.4 to 0.6). Selective breeding over three generations showed increasing divergence between high and low responder lines (Cohen's d = 0.89 in second generation to d = 1.64 in third generation).
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C43-C48 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B. The heritability analysis is appropriately designed and executed, with statistical support (Shapiro-Wilks test, Cohen's d effect sizes). The increasing effect size across generations provides strong evidence for genetic contribution to nicotine CPP behavior.

results.result: Out of 30 ENU-mutagenized families screened for CPP, individuals from nine families were in the top 5% and five families in the bottom 5% of the distribution. Exome sequencing identified 25 nonsense and essential splice site mutations. Of these, only slit3sa1569/+ (splice acceptor site disruption) segregated with increased nicotine preference in the AJBQM1 family. No mutations in AJBQM2 segregated with the phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53, C102-C103 are supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4A and Supplementary file 1. The screening strategy is well-designed, and the segregation analysis appropriately identifies slit3 as the causal gene. The use of exome sequencing and systematic genotyping of candidate mutations is rigorous.

results.result: The association between slit3 loss of function and increased nicotine preference was confirmed using an independent zebrafish mutant line (slit3sa202) with a different loss of function mutation. Heterozygous slit3sa202 fish showed enhanced nicotine CPP (p=0.03) compared to wild type siblings. Both mutations (slit3sa1569 affecting splicing at amino acid 176, slit3sa202 introducing premature stop at amino acid 163) reside before the second LRR domain essential for ROBO receptor interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58, C104, C126 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and appropriately cited literature (Brose et al., 1999). The independent confirmation with a second allele is a critical strength of the study, providing strong evidence that slit3 loss of function causes increased nicotine preference. The molecular characterization of both alleles is appropriate.

results.result: SLIT3 is a member of a family of axon guidance proteins previously suggested to be involved in dopaminergic and serotonergic pathfinding. However, immunostaining analysis revealed no significant differences between slit3sa1569 mutant and wild type larvae in the number of serotonergic (5-HT) or catecholaminergic (TH) cells in multiple brain regions, nor in the number of TH-labeled axon tracts projecting to the midline. No obvious differences were observed in anti-acetylated tubulin staining along the midline in the ventral forebrain.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C67, C35 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, with appropriate citations (Smidt and Burbach, 2007; Miyasaka et al., 2005). The immunohistochemical analysis is thorough, examining multiple brain regions and using appropriate controls. The lack of gross pathfinding defects is clearly documented with quantitative data and statistical analysis.

results.result: Acoustic startle response analysis revealed that habituation to acoustic startle involves catecholamine signaling and is associated with addiction vulnerability in humans. In drug-free conditions, 68% of wild type fish responded to the first stimulus, decreasing to 16% for the last stimulus, with no differences across slit3sa1569 genotypes. However, with amisulpride treatment, wild types showed a biphasic dose-dependent effect (0.05 mg/L increased responses, 0.5 mg/L decreased responses), while homozygous slit3sa1569 mutants showed no significant dose effect. A significant three-way interaction (genotype × dose × stimulus number, p=0.04) confirmed differential sensitivity. Differences in startle behavior were not confounded by differences in locomotion.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C86 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, with appropriate citations (Quednow et al., 2006; Loeber et al., 2007; Vrana et al., 2015; Kumari and Gray, 1999; Rankin et al., 2009). The acoustic startle analysis is well-designed with appropriate controls and statistical analysis. The differential response to amisulpride between genotypes provides functional evidence for altered dopaminergic/serotonergic signaling in slit3 mutants.

results.result: Adult slit3sa1569/sa1569 mutant zebrafish showed qualitatively different responses to amisulpride inhibition of CPP compared to wild type siblings. The minimal CPP induced by 5 μM nicotine in wild type fish was prevented by pre-exposure to 0.5 mg/L amisulpride, but nicotine-induced CPP in slit3sa1569 homozygous mutants was not affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89, C157 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7. The differential sensitivity to amisulpride in adult fish is consistent with the larval startle response data, providing convergent evidence for persistent alterations in dopaminergic/serotonergic signaling in slit3 mutants across developmental stages.

results.result: Gene expression analysis revealed that only htr1aa showed a significant difference in expression across genotypes after correcting for multiple testing ([F(2,6)=44], p=0.0003), with increased expression in slit3 mutant larvae. Several other genes (drd3, chrnb3, htr4, adra2b) showed nominal significance but did not survive multiple testing correction.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C34 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and Supplementary file 1H. The qPCR analysis is appropriately conducted with proper statistical correction for multiple testing. The specific upregulation of htr1aa is a key finding that provides molecular insight into the mechanism underlying the behavioral phenotype.

results.result: Analysis of the SLIT3 locus in the London cohort identified two SNPs in high linkage disequilibrium (rs12654448 and rs17734503) associated with cigarette consumption (p=0.00125 and p=0.00227). In heavy smokers, these SNPs plus rs11742567 were associated with consumption. The SNP rs11742567 was associated with consumption in light smokers (p=0.003909) and with quitting. The minor alleles were associated with fewer cigarettes smoked per day and with smoking cessation. No other SLIT3 polymorphisms were associated with smoking initiation, persistent smoking, or cessation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96, C36-C37, C105-C106 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9 and Table 1. The human genetic analysis is appropriately conducted with correction for multiple comparisons using Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. The associations are consistent across different smoking phenotypes and provide translational validation of the zebrafish findings.

results.result: In the Finnish twins cohort, associations were observed between rs17734503 and DSM-IV nicotine dependence symptoms (p=0.0322) and age at onset of weekly smoking (p=0.00116), and between rs12654448 and age at onset of weekly smoking (p=0.00105). The same SLIT3 alleles identified in the London cohort were associated with DSM-IV nicotine dependence symptoms and age at onset of weekly smoking.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99, C107-C108 are supported by experimental data shown in Table 2. The replication in an independent cohort with more detailed smoking phenotypes strengthens the evidence for SLIT3's role in smoking behavior. The consistency of associations across cohorts and phenotypes is notable.

results.result: The SNPs rs12654448 and rs17734503 are in non-coding domains, and no evidence of affecting gene expression was found in the GTEx database.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by analysis of SNP location and GTEx database queries. This is an important limitation that prevents prediction of loss or gain of function from SNP location alone. The lack of eQTL effects suggests the variants may affect regulation through other mechanisms.

results.result: The study demonstrates that zebrafish can be used to identify genes associated with smoking behavior in humans. Variants in the SLIT3 gene are linked in humans with disruption of SLIT3 function that may affect propensity to develop tobacco dependence. The results provide evidence for a role for SLIT3 in regulating smoking behavior in humans and confirm adult zebrafish as a translationally relevant animal model for addiction-related behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110, C38, C217-C218 represent the main conclusions of the study and are supported by the convergent evidence from zebrafish genetics, behavioral analysis, and human genetic associations. The successful translation from zebrafish to human genetics is a major strength. However, the mechanistic link between SLIT3 variants and function in humans remains speculative (C110 includes speculation).

results.result: The study suggests that SLIT3 signaling plays a role in the development of dopaminergic and serotonergic pathways affecting behaviors associated with nicotine sensitivity. The findings of increased htr1aa expression, altered sensitivity to amisulpride, and altered nicotine CPP support this role.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C158-C159, C199 represent mechanistic interpretations that are partially supported but remain speculative. While the behavioral and gene expression data are solid, the lack of detectable anatomical differences in dopaminergic/serotonergic pathways (C61-C67) creates uncertainty about the developmental mechanism. The increased htr1aa expression and altered amisulpride sensitivity suggest functional differences, but the precise developmental role of SLIT3 in these pathways remains to be established. Additional experiments examining circuit formation at different developmental stages would be needed to fully support these claims.

results.result: The screening approach using ENU-mutagenized zebrafish families followed by sibling re-screen is a proof of principle study indicating the relevance of zebrafish for human studies. The approach emphasizes the advantage of first using a screen with a low number of individuals per family to increase efficiency. This is the first report of a forward behavioral genetic screen in adult zebrafish successfully predicting a novel human coding genetic region involved in a complex human behavioral trait.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C115, C118, C216 are supported by the successful identification of slit3 and its validation in human cohorts. The methodological innovation of screening small numbers from many families is well-justified by the results. The claim of being the first such report (C216) is appropriately qualified with 'to our knowledge' and represents a significant methodological advance.

results.result: A limitation of the forward genetic approach is that many genes are duplicated in zebrafish due to teleost tetraploidization, and ENU-mutagenesis in one copy may not be sufficient to produce behavioral changes due to genetic compensation. However, slit3 is present as a single copy, which may have facilitated identification of its role. The most significant consequence of tetraploidization is temporal and spatial specific expression of gene duplicates, which may offset concerns regarding compensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C125 appropriately discuss limitations and advantages of the zebrafish model. The discussion of gene duplication is based on established knowledge about zebrafish genome evolution. The speculation about how single-copy status facilitated identification (C123) and how differential expression may offset compensation concerns (C125) is reasonable but remains speculative.

results.result: SLIT molecules bind to ROBO receptors through a conserved LRR domain. The mutations in slit3sa1569 (truncation at amino acid 176) and slit3sa202 (truncation at amino acid 163) are immediately adjacent to the LRR2 domain and would be predicted to lead to non-functional proteins. SLIT proteins are expressed in many tissues and play major roles in developmental processes. Despite neuronal expression, the most prominent phenotype in Slit3 deficient mice is diaphragmatic hernia with no obvious neuronal defects reported. Overlap with other slit molecules may compensate for loss of slit3 in the brain, though subtle differences in circuit formation may have escaped detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C140 provide appropriate molecular and biological context for interpreting the results, with proper citations (Morlot et al., 2007; Blockus and Chédotal, 2014; Marillat et al., 2002; Yuan et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2003; Long et al., 2004). The discussion of potential compensation and subtle effects is appropriately speculative.

results.result: The acoustic startle response is associated with addiction vulnerability and sensitive to dopaminergic antagonists in zebrafish and mammals. Although amisulpride binding affinity in zebrafish has not been examined, behavioral effects are consistent with mammalian binding characteristics. In mammals, amisulpride binds D2/3 receptors with greater affinity at presynaptic than postsynaptic receptors. Treatment with D2/3 antagonists leads to biphasic effects on locomotion in both rodents and zebrafish, suggesting similar binding affinities and receptor properties. High amisulpride concentrations increased habituation in wild type fish, consistent with human effects, and the biphasic dose-response suggests involvement of both pre- and post-synaptic dopamine receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C153 provide appropriate pharmacological context with proper citations (Quednow et al., 2006; Halberstadt and Geyer, 2009; Burgess and Granato, 2007; Tran et al., 2015; Schoemaker et al., 1997; Perrault et al., 1997; Beaulieu and Gainetdinov, 2011; Millan et al., 2004). The inference about similar binding properties in zebrafish based on behavioral effects is reasonable but remains indirect evidence.

results.result: slit3sa1569 mutant larvae showed decreased habituation in the presence of both high and low dose amisulpride, suggesting reduced sensitivity to amisulpride at post-synaptic sites, possibly related to the marginal increase in dopamine D3 receptors in slit3 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 are partially supported by the startle response data (Figure 6), but the mechanistic interpretation (C155-C156) is speculative. The link to D3 receptor upregulation is particularly uncertain since drd3 expression showed only nominal significance that did not survive multiple testing correction. The interpretation would be strengthened by additional experiments directly testing D3 receptor function.

results.result: Differential sensitivity to amisulpride actions at serotonergic receptors cannot be ruled out. Amisulpride acts as an antagonist at Htr7 and Htr2b receptors with affinities approximately four times lower than at dopaminergic receptors. In mice, acoustic startle is sensitive to inhibition at Htr2b sites, and genetic ablation of Htr2b induced reduced startle amplitude and deficits in prepulse inhibition. Loss of Htr7 has no effect on acoustic startle in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C164 appropriately discuss alternative interpretations with proper citations (Pitychoutis et al., 2015; Semenova et al., 2008). This discussion acknowledges the complexity of amisulpride's pharmacology and the difficulty in definitively attributing effects to dopaminergic versus serotonergic mechanisms.

results.result: The observation of increased htr1aa expression in slit3 mutants is of interest given the established links between serotonergic signaling and drug reward. HTR1A is the major inhibitory serotonergic receptor in mammals, present as autoreceptors in the raphe and heteroreceptors in mood/anxiety-related brain regions. Interactions between HTR1A and dopaminergic signaling are well established. HTR1A is upregulated in conditions of reduced serotonergic signaling, and loss of serotonergic signaling from the DRN affects dopaminergic axonal outgrowth in a stage-specific manner. The overlapping expression of slit3 and htr1aa in the posterior raphe nucleus supports interaction between these systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C198 provide extensive discussion of HTR1A biology and its potential relevance to the findings, with numerous appropriate citations (Fletcher et al., 2008; Olausson et al., 2002; Roberts et al., 1994; LeMarquand et al., 1994; Opitz and Weischer, 1988; Dao et al., 2011; Seth et al., 2002; Rasmussen et al., 1997, 2000; Harrison et al., 2001; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2014; Bantick et al., 2001; Ichikawa et al., 1995; Newman-Tancredi, 2010, 2011; Łukasiewicz et al., 2016; Carrard et al., 2011; Shi et al., 2004; Glessner et al., 2010; Cukier et al., 2014; Chen et al., 1998; Benes et al., 2000; Miyasaka et al., 2005; Norton et al., 2008; Boehmler et al., 2004; Ackerman and Boyd, 2016). This extensive discussion provides valuable context for interpreting the htr1aa upregulation finding.

results.result: The study has several limitations: zebrafish of various ages were used in different experiments, which confirms that slit3 loss-of-function alters behavior from early life to adulthood but mechanisms may differ. Whole embryos were used for qPCR, so changes in non-neuronal tissue may contribute and expression in one tissue may mask changes in another. Only a limited number of receptors and transporters were examined, so important differences in other pathways may have been missed.
results.evaluation: Claims C200-C206 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the study. These are reasonable concerns that do not invalidate the main findings but suggest areas for future investigation. The acknowledgment of limitations strengthens the overall credibility of the work.

results.result: The translational effects of SLIT3 gene variants were confirmed in a human study and validated in a second independent cohort. The sample sizes are small compared to discovery studies, but the studies validated zebrafish findings and analyzed only a small set of SNPs focused on one gene, minimizing type one error. Analyses were corrected for multiple comparisons. The Finnish cohort explored effects on richer smoking phenotypes rather than formal replication. Associations between SLIT3 and smoking phenotypes have been found in previous GWAS, but larger studies would be needed for greater precision on effect size estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C214 appropriately discuss the human genetic studies and their limitations. The acknowledgment of small sample sizes is important, but the focused candidate gene approach and use of two independent cohorts provide reasonable support for the associations. The citation to previous GWAS findings (Watanabe et al., 2019) provides additional context.

results.result: Further studies are required to determine the effects of genetic variation in SLIT3 on anatomical pathways in the human brain and their functioning. Further work analyzing cellular processes affected by the slit3 mutation may provide useful targets for designing tailored treatments to aid smoking cessation.
results.evaluation: Claims C215, C219 appropriately suggest future research directions. These are reasonable extensions of the current work that would strengthen the translational implications of the findings.
